video_title: Paul Kedrosky: Nvidia Is Now the AI Bubble's Single Point of Failure
gist: Paul Kedrosky argues the AI capex boom is historically unusual because it sits at the multiplicative intersection of four classic bubble forces (technology, credit, government policy, real estate), with Nvidia now the single point of failure through circular financing across OpenAI, Microsoft, and CoreWeave; he expects rapid LLM commoditization to collapse token pricing and crush the debt-funded neoclouds, while favoring semiconductor bottleneck plays (ASML, TSMC) and multi-model hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google) over single-model bets like OpenAI and Anthropic.

themes.theme: The AI capex bubble: four forces converging multiplicatively

insights.claim: The current AI data-center capex boom is unusual among historical US non-residential fixed investment surges (canals, railroads, electrification, WWII rearmament, fiber optics) because it sits at the intersection of four distinct bubble-driving forces at once — a powerful technology story, a loose-credit/financing story, a government policy story (US-China tech competition), and a speculative real-estate story — and the interaction of these forces is multiplicative and geometric rather than merely additive, making this moment unusually precarious.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Investors should not evaluate AI capex risk through a single lens (e.g., just credit risk or just tech-cycle risk); the compounding interaction of credit, real estate, policy, and tech hype means downside scenarios could cascade faster and more severely than in past single-factor bubbles.
insights.quote: the intersection of all their forces isn't just additive it's multiplicative and geometric and that's why this moment is so precarious and unusual

insights.claim: AI-related data center capex is currently responsible for roughly 30-60% of US GDP growth depending on the quarter, and data-center spending has crowded out nearly all other categories of commercial fixed investment.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: US headline GDP growth is now highly dependent on a single, narrow, debt- and credit-sensitive investment category; any slowdown in AI capex would have an outsized, direct impact on reported GDP growth, not just tech-sector earnings.
insights.quote: AI capex broadly is like... anywhere from 30 to 60% of GDP growth in the United States, which is bonkers

insights.claim: In historical infrastructure buildouts like railroads, roughly 50% of all track miles ever laid were eventually abandoned even though rail freight volumes ultimately exceeded early-era levels decades later — meaning the technology thesis proved correct long-term even as the specific capital that funded the initial buildout was largely destroyed.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Being right about AI's long-term societal importance does not protect current-era AI infrastructure investors from severe capital destruction — expect a wave of asset write-offs/bankruptcies among today's specific capex financiers even if AI itself succeeds as a technology, much like WorldCom/JDS Uniphase during the fiber buildout.
insights.quote: something like 50% of all railroad track miles ever laid were eventually abandoned but we still ship more stuff via railroads than we ever did. It just meant that it was a really shitty investment

insights.claim: More than half of hyperscaler spending on data centers is now externally financed (via SPVs and off-balance-sheet vehicles) rather than funded from operating cash flow, a reversal from the earlier era when bulls argued hyperscalers' strong credit ratings and cash flow made the buildout self-evidently safe.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: The 'these are prime credits, so it's fine' argument for AI capex safety no longer applies once financing shifts off-balance-sheet; credit markets are increasingly underwriting the data centers themselves rather than the hyperscaler parent, exposing investors to a structurally different (and historically riskier) risk profile.
insights.quote: more than half of spending on hyperscaler spending on data centers is now externally financed whether it's through SPVs and off balance sheet

insights.claim: Capital markets have a well-documented pattern of eventually turning prime credits into subprime credits by extending them enough time and leverage, and this is the mechanism now playing out in AI data center financing, similar to the pre-2008 subprime mortgage securitization era's 'I'll be gone, you'll be gone' (IBGYBG) originate-and-distribute incentive structure.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: The AI data-center debt market is exhibiting the same agency/incentive misalignment that preceded the 2008 financial crisis — sell-side structurers earn fees without warehousing risk, meaning credit quality embedded in AI infrastructure debt should be treated with the same skepticism as pre-crisis structured mortgage products.
insights.quote: capital markets are very good at turning prime credits into subprime credits. They just give them enough time and I they'll walk you there.

insights.claim: 'Powered shells' — speculative data center real estate developments with no signed customers and no installed GPUs, built purely on access to water/power at a site by numbered holding companies hoping to attract tenants later — are proliferating as a distinct speculative real-estate layer within the AI buildout.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: This is a concrete, checkable red flag of late-cycle speculative excess in AI infrastructure — investors should treat announcements of new data center sites without disclosed anchor tenants or hardware commitments as speculative land plays, not committed AI capacity.
insights.quote: data centers that actually have no customers and have no GPUs. It's just somebody got access to water power in a site and they build in a speculative basis hoping that one day they can get tenants

themes.theme: Nvidia as the single point of failure via circular financing

insights.claim: Nvidia's roughly half-a-trillion-dollar financing pool deal (involving Goldman Sachs' David Solomon, Blackstone, BlackRock, Brookfield, and other partners) creates a new 'GPU compute' asset class in which participants effectively backstop up to 25% of the value of GPUs, putting institutional balance sheets directly at risk to prop up used/depreciating GPU values — a move the guest reads as defensive rather than a confident bet, and calls 'bonkers.'
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: A deal explicitly designed to backstop GPU resale values signals that sophisticated financial players see real risk of GPU value depreciation/oversupply — worth monitoring as a leading indicator of stress in the broader AI hardware financing complex, and a caution against assuming GPU-backed debt structures are low-risk collateral.
insights.quote: they're backstopping, you know, up to 25%... putting their balance sheet at risk... I thought it was more defensive in a way than offensive

insights.claim: Nvidia's acquisition of Hugging Face is framed as a backward-integration move to control AI model distribution, analogous to hyperscalers ('the Greeks' in an extended 'The Wire' analogy) controlling supply, since Nvidia and other players increasingly realize the real leverage sits with whoever controls distribution and infrastructure access, not just compute supply.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Watch for continued vertical/backward integration moves by Nvidia and other infrastructure suppliers into model distribution and hosting layers, as competition shifts from GPU supply scarcity toward control of the full stack.
insights.quote: Hugging Face is just a distribution channel... it's inevitable that everything backwards integrates and the conflict becomes... the hyperscalers

insights.claim: Nvidia is identified as the AI ecosystem's single point of failure because it simultaneously acts as GPU supplier, an investor/backstop in customers like OpenAI, and now (via deals and acquisitions) a distribution/model layer participant — meaning any shock to sovereign policy (export restrictions), credit markets, or GPU resale pricing flows directly back onto Nvidia's own balance sheet and equity.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Concentrated single-stock risk in Nvidia is now systemic to the entire AI capex ecosystem, not just an Nvidia-specific earnings risk — a broad AI-exposure portfolio has more correlated tail risk to Nvidia-specific shocks (export policy, credit, GPU oversupply) than headline diversification suggests.
insights.quote: they are increasingly like the line I use is that failure is overdetermined here. There's lots of ways this whole thing can break... a really obvious single point of failure remains Nvidia

insights.claim: A circular financing chain links Nvidia, OpenAI, Microsoft, and CoreWeave: Nvidia is a major investor in OpenAI and supplies GPUs to CoreWeave (a private company effectively dependent on Nvidia); OpenAI is a major customer of Microsoft Azure while Microsoft is a major OpenAI investor; and Microsoft is CoreWeave's largest customer — creating a closed loop where the same capital and demand are effectively being recycled and double-counted across the ecosystem.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky / Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Reported AI ecosystem revenue and demand figures likely overstate genuine end-market demand due to this circularity; investors should discount headline 'contracted revenue' or 'partnership' announcements between these four entities as partially self-referential rather than independent validation of demand.
insights.quote: if Nvidia doesn't exist, right? So, they're their largest investor and Coreweave gets basically all of their GPUs, right, from uh Nvidia and then Microsoft is Coreweave's largest customer

insights.claim: If AI token demand growth slows (e.g., due to coding-market saturation), the neoclouds (marginal GPU capacity providers like CoreWeave) would be the first entities left holding the bag, since they are the marginal suppliers of excess capacity most reliant on external debt financing and have fixed debt obligations regardless of demand realization.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: A specific, monitorable prediction: neocloud debt and equity (CoreWeave and similar GPU-rental-focused companies) are the highest-risk instruments in the AI capex chain if demand growth decelerates — a candidate short thesis or at minimum a name to avoid relative to core hyperscalers.
insights.quote: the first folks that are going to be left holding the bag are the Neoclouds. Like, let's just be clear. Hands, hands down, no question.

insights.claim: OpenAI has reportedly committed to roughly $1.5 trillion worth of infrastructure/compute contracts without currently having the capital to fund them, ahead of an anticipated IPO around Q1 2027 (after Anthropic's).
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: OpenAI's committed contract obligations far exceed its current funding, implying continued heavy reliance on future capital raises (equity or debt) to meet contractual commitments — a key funding/dilution and counterparty risk to track ahead of its rumored 2027 IPO.
insights.quote: Open AAI, you know, they've thrown around what a$1.5 trillion dollars worth of contracts. They don't really have the money to do it, right?

themes.theme: LLM commoditization: converging models, collapsing token prices

insights.claim: Large language models are rapidly converging in capability (evidenced by narrowing variance on indices like the Epoch Capabilities Index) even as models improve overall, analogous to Stephen Jay Gould's explanation for why .400 hitters disappeared from baseball — not because players got worse, but because the whole talent distribution's variance collapsed as everyone converged toward similar performance.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: As model quality differentiation shrinks, frontier labs lose the ability to charge a quality premium — investors should expect continued price compression across the LLM market and should be skeptical of any single model's ability to sustain outsized pricing power for long.
insights.quote: the exact same thing is happening in large language models... it's like 400 hitters in baseball... everyone's getting better, but the variance is collapsing

insights.claim: Frontier proprietary LLMs currently price at roughly 5-50x per-token cost compared to Chinese open-weight models, but this pricing premium ('pricing halo') is compressing quickly as the practical performance gap narrows, and frontier labs' publicized cybersecurity/safety disclosures (e.g., 'we broke Hugging Face,' 'we broke X') function partly as negative marketing to protect that eroding price premium rather than purely as safety transparency.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Discount some portion of AI safety/danger disclosures from frontier labs as marketing designed to justify premium pricing rather than purely objective risk transparency; expect the 5-50x pricing premium over open-weight alternatives to continue eroding, pressuring frontier lab gross margins.
insights.quote: frontier models are still anywhere from 5 to 50x as expensive on a per token basis as the Chinese open source openweight models and that margin is coming down very very quickly

insights.claim: Anthropic's public positioning that its models are 'the safest' while simultaneously warning they could eliminate roughly 50% of jobs represents a difficult-to-reconcile moral contradiction, which the guest interprets as evidence that much of this 'doom' messaging functions as attention-grabbing negative marketing in a crowded, hard-to-differentiate AI marketplace rather than a fully consistent ethical stance.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Investors and policymakers should treat AI labs' public doom/safety messaging with some skepticism as a marketing and differentiation tool, separate from assessing the technology's actual economic disruption risk, which the guest still views as real and consequential.
insights.quote: this kind of almost doombased marketing. If you genuinely believe that we're producing the safest models, but you also believe it's going to take away 50% of jobs, these are two difficult things to reconcile

insights.claim: AI tokens are described as the first truly hyperdeflationary commodity in economic history, with performance-adjusted token prices falling 50-80% year-over-year, meaning an AI company must grow unit volume by roughly 500-1,000% annually just to hold revenue flat — a scale of required growth far beyond what public-market growth expectations (e.g., ~50% YoY for a newly public Anthropic) can realistically satisfy.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: This is a hard quantitative ceiling on AI lab revenue growth given deflationary unit economics — investors modeling frontier AI lab revenue trajectories (ahead of expected IPOs) should stress-test whether projected volume growth can plausibly offset 50-80% annual price declines, since the required growth rate (500-1000%) is likely unsustainable.
insights.quote: with anywhere from 500 to a,000% you're going to have to sell just to stand still. You have to grow that fast year over year just to stay in the same frigin place

insights.claim: As token prices race toward marginal cost of production due to commoditization, the large and increasingly externally-financed debt loads backing AI infrastructure (e.g., Oracle's data-center-related debt) will face repricing pressure at future refinancing/rollover dates, similar to the repricing cascade seen during the 2008 financial crisis.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Debt rollover dates for major AI infrastructure issuers (Oracle cited as an example) are concrete future catalysts to watch — expect a 'rolling series of repricings and failures' as commoditized token economics collide with fixed debt service obligations struck under more optimistic pricing assumptions.
insights.quote: you're going to see, I think, a rolling series of repricings and failures as a result of this... predictable commoditization

insights.claim: Google's TPUs reportedly introduced a technique this week compressing key-value cache sequences by a factor of roughly 6-8x, sharply reducing memory requirements for inference — part of a broader wave of new architectures emerging across the industry (including a related Microsoft announcement) specifically engineered to reduce dependence on expensive high-bandwidth memory (HBM), which will reduce future demand for the newest-generation GPUs.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Emerging memory-efficient inference architectures are a direct, near-term (12-month horizon) threat to Nvidia's high-margin GPU/HBM demand — investors extrapolating Nvidia's historical GPU attach-rate and memory demand forward should factor in imminent architectural workarounds designed explicitly to reduce that dependency.
insights.quote: changing the way that they compress some of the... key value sequences inside the models into like a factor of like six or seven or eight which will sharply reduce the amount of memory required

insights.claim: At least two major Chinese memory manufacturers are each independently planning to add roughly 'a Samsung's worth' of memory production capacity between now and early 2028, which the guest likens to the export-driven collapse in solar panel prices and expects to similarly crater memory (and by extension GPU-adjacent) pricing.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: A memory supply glut driven by Chinese capacity additions (comparable in scale to the solar panel price collapse) is a specific, dated (by 2028) catalyst that could sharply compress memory pricing and pressure the earnings of memory suppliers (Micron, SK Hynix, Samsung) and, indirectly, Nvidia's bundled hardware economics.
insights.quote: some of the largest Chinese memory manufacturers... are both showing numbers that suggest they essentially want to add a Samsung's worth of capacity over the next 12 months... between now and early... 2028

insights.claim: Despite beating and raising every quarter for over two years, Nvidia trades at only about 17.5x earnings, and semiconductor stocks broadly (SOX index down ~25%, Micron's HBM pricing having round-tripped from 100 to 1200 to down ~25% off highs) are behaving as if the market is discounting a coming supply glut and price collapse, even as mega-cap tech ('Mag 7') stocks rally as relatively defensive due to their superior access to cheap capital.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: The market (via Nvidia's compressed earnings multiple and SOX underperformance) is already partially pricing in the memory/GPU oversupply and margin compression thesis, suggesting a chip-sector-wide derating is underway even as headline earnings beats continue — a divergence worth watching between reported fundamentals and multiple compression.
insights.quote: it trades at 17 and a half times earnings... Micron... was to your point about sold out supply demand scenario as far as HBM goes from 100 to 1200 in a year and now it's come off about 25%

themes.theme: Coding-driven adoption is not representative of future AI demand

insights.claim: The last four years of AI adoption have been driven overwhelmingly by software engineers/coders as the dominant use case, but coders are structurally unrepresentative of the broader white-collar labor market because coding has a 'steep gradient descent' (code either works or visibly breaks, giving fast, clear feedback that enables safe agentic automation) and is 'expansive' (a short prompt generates large token volumes), unlike most white-collar tasks (summarizing, emailing, PowerPoints) which are 'compressive' (large inputs condensed to short outputs) and tolerate no reliable self-correcting signal.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Current AI revenue/usage projections built by extrapolating from coding-driven token consumption are likely to badly overstate future demand once the far larger, but lower-token, compressive white-collar use cases dominate adoption — a structural reason to be skeptical of AI labs' aggressive multi-year revenue growth targets.
insights.quote: coders are wildly unrepresentative of the mass market of adoption... projections I'm making today based on the current trajectory of token usage are at the very best fraught and probably wrong

insights.claim: The coding tools market is already approaching saturation — it is very hard to find a professional coder not already using AI coding tools — meaning the historically dominant growth driver for token consumption is running out of new users to add, even as capex has been built out as if the last four years of coding-driven growth would extrapolate for the next twenty.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Watch for a visible deceleration in token-usage growth over roughly the next 12 months as coding-market saturation becomes apparent in AI labs' usage data — this is a specific, near-term falsifiable prediction relevant to Anthropic/OpenAI revenue growth assumptions ahead of their IPOs.
insights.quote: we're already at the point of sort of mass adoption. It's very hard to find a coder who's not already using these tools... we've built capacity capex spending as if the last four years are the next 20 and that's clearly not the case

insights.claim: Speculative future high-token-volume use cases like humanoid robots (with one industry report reportedly raising its unit forecast roughly 5x, from about 1 billion to 5 billion units) are cited by bulls to justify continued infrastructure buildout, but the guest argues this reasoning is a fallacy ('if my aunt had wheels, she'd be a bicycle') because it discounts speculative demand that is likely a decade or more away into current capital allocation decisions, reflecting poor understanding of how capital markets actually price risk.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of AI infrastructure bull cases that lean on distant, unproven demand sources (humanoid robotics, ambient computing) to justify near-term capex; discounting decade-plus-away demand into today's valuation is a red flag for speculative excess rather than sound capital allocation.
insights.quote: you're asking me to grant something that isn't even 10 years away. And then in turn discounted into my current model... it just shows a poor understanding of how capital markets work

themes.theme: Where to hide: multi-model hyperscalers and semiconductor bottlenecks

insights.claim: Microsoft, Amazon (AWS), and Google are structurally better-positioned than single-model bets like OpenAI or Anthropic because they are becoming model-agnostic 'Costco of large language models' — hosting multiple converging, commoditizing models and monetizing via enterprise-grade availability, security, and integration rather than betting on any one model's superiority, avoiding the 'specialty store' risk of over-committing to a single, potentially-displaced model provider.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Favor diversified, multi-model hyperscaler exposure (Microsoft, Amazon, Google) over single-model-dependent companies (OpenAI, Anthropic) as the safer way to capture AI monetization while models continue to commoditize and converge in capability.
insights.quote: Microsoft is much and AWS and Google and so on, they're much more like the Costco of this stuff... models are converging, homogenizing, becoming price driven

insights.claim: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's public statement that the company is now 'energy constrained' rather than compute/capacity constrained is interpreted as evidence Microsoft has shifted from training large frontier models to hosting other companies' models within its Copilot products, effectively monetizing inference rather than training compute.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Microsoft's business model is shifting toward being an inference/hosting layer (higher-margin, more model-agnostic) rather than a training-compute consumer, supporting the thesis that diversified hyperscalers capture AI value more durably than frontier model developers.
insights.quote: Satcha Nadella... said that I'm no longer capacity constrained or compute constrained... I am energy constrained

insights.claim: The current market sentiment around large language models is compared to the 'iPhone 5' moment in smartphone history — early model releases (like early iPhones) delivered genuinely dramatic step-change improvements, but subsequent releases show diminishing, converging gains, even though a subset of enthusiasts (compared to Reddit AI-acceleration communities awaiting 'infinite abundance') continue to treat each new model release as a major event; the broader market consensus has not yet caught up to this convergence reality.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Investors and the media narrative are still overreacting to individual model release announcements as major catalysts; the guest's 'meta-observation' is that this excitement is increasingly disconnected from actual differentiated capability, implying diminishing trading/valuation impact from future frontier model launches.
insights.quote: we're still in this iPhone 5 kind of moment... these things have stopped changing so dramatically. You don't really need to care anymore

insights.claim: Google is flagged as an underappreciated, broadly diversified way to invest in the AI theme given roughly seven owned properties with 2+ billion users each (some approaching 3 billion), vertical integration into custom TPU silicon avoiding full Nvidia dependence, and large amounts of still under-monetized proprietary data — despite recent organizational turnover, and it trades at a relatively reasonable valuation compared to pure-play AI names.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan / Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Google is presented as a lower-risk, reasonably-valued way to gain broad AI exposure relative to pure-play, single-model bets — a candidate long idea for investors seeking AI upside without frontier-model-specific risk.
insights.quote: they still sit on some of the most valuable assets and some of the most undermonetized data... I couldn't agree more

insights.claim: The guest argues the real structural scarcity worth investing behind is not software or models (which are becoming commoditized and 'ubiquitous, cheap, free') but the physical bottom of the semiconductor stack — extreme ultraviolet lithography, wafer fabrication — pointing to ASML, TSMC (at the right price), and emerging Chinese memory makers like CXMT as the names best positioned at genuine points of structural scarcity.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: A concrete long-idea framework: rotate AI exposure away from software/model layers (converging, commoditizing) and toward physical chip-manufacturing bottleneck suppliers (ASML, TSMC) where genuine technical scarcity and pricing power persist.
insights.quote: the people that I'm most interested in are people who are helping to do that. ASNL is a good example... what's still hard is ultraviolet lithography

insights.claim: A Zeiss executive publicly claimed China remains roughly 15 years behind in high-line-density extreme ultraviolet lithography competitiveness, but the guest disagrees with that timeline, believing China (alongside the US) is investing ferociously to close that gap much faster than 15 years.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Don't assume the ASML/TSMC lithography moat versus China is a multi-decade certainty — the guest's view that China is closing the EUV gap faster than the 15-year consensus estimate is a risk factor for the long-term durability of Western lithography monopoly pricing power.
insights.quote: arguing that China is still 15 years from being able to be competitive at the really high line density ultraiththography. I don't think that's true

insights.claim: The 'SaaS apocalypse' narrative (that AI-generated/'vibe-coded' software would make enterprise SaaS incumbents obsolete) is dismissed as fundamentally mistaken, because enterprises buy SaaS not because building software is technically hard but because they want an external vendor to blame or sue when something breaks, rather than owning that operational and reputational risk themselves — a dynamic that AI-driven ease of coding does not change.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Fade the 'AI kills SaaS incumbents' bear thesis; incumbent SaaS vendors with reputations may actually strengthen their competitive position as AI floods the market with low-differentiation vibe-coded alternatives that enterprises don't trust for accountability reasons.
insights.quote: the reason why people buy enterprise SAS is not because it's hard... it's because they don't want to do it and they want someone else to either shout at or sue when it doesn't work

insights.claim: Even though the SaaS apocalypse thesis is wrong on existential-risk grounds, the guest still expects continued price and margin compression across SaaS as AI-driven competition and commoditization pressure pricing, without producing an actual wave of incumbent failures.
insights.speaker: Paul Kedrosky
insights.so_what: Model SaaS incumbents for continued gradual margin compression rather than a discrete competitive collapse — a nuanced middle-ground view distinct from both aggressive AI-disruption bears and complacent SaaS bulls.
insights.quote: you're going to see price and margin compression, but the idea that they're at some kind of existential risk is ridiculous

insights.claim: Palantir is cited as an example of a stock that traded like 'the bubble stock of all bubble stocks,' commanding hundreds of billions in market cap on the strength of its AI platform (AIP) narrative despite only about $7 billion in revenue.
insights.speaker: Dan Nathan
insights.so_what: Palantir's market cap-to-revenue disconnect (hundreds of billions in value against ~$7B revenue) is flagged as a specific, checkable example of speculative excess within AI-adjacent software valuations worth monitoring for a re-rating.
insights.quote: this was, you know, AIP, like literally AI platform... this was the thing that was drawing hundreds of billions of dollars in market cap despite that they have like a $7 billion revenue base
